arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Bullock argued the case tests eminent domain limits. He stated every home produces more revenue if it becomes a mall.
Mr. Horton argued the takings clause provides just compensation. He stated two reasons against a specific legal standard.
Justice Breyer noted private use always has some public benefit. He cited increasing jobs or taxes as examples.
Justice O'Connor asked if the Court has ever found a limit exceeded. She referenced the Berman opinion on legislative determinations.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The case tests the limits of the Fifth Amendment. It asks if a city can take private property for private use. The city claims this action boosts local jobs and taxes. the sides that brought the case claim this violates the public use requirement.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the sides that brought the case want the Court to strike down the seizure. They argue private development is not a public use.
The city wants the Court to uphold the seizure. It argues economic growth serves the public interest.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the sides that brought the case argue the Fifth Amendment limits eminent domain power. They claim private profit is not a public use.
The city argues economic revitalization is a public purpose. It claims this action creates jobs and tax revenue.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Ginsburg asked if the depressed economy distinguishes this case. She noted the city wanted to build up the community.
Justice Scalia asked if elevating a depressed city is a better justification. He compared this to making a prosperous city more prosperous.
